segments.title: Military necessity and the waste of life
segments.summary: The opening separates unavoidable wartime sacrifice from an operation too small and poorly planned to achieve its stated aims.
segments.body: Tan No. 2 was an ethical failure because it had no viable military purpose. States may have to fight when aggression threatens others, but commanders still owe their personnel a credible objective. The assigned force was too small, and the plan offered no plausible route to success. That judgment does not erase the cultural, social, economic, and historiographical reasons Japan adopted kamikaze operations.

evidence.note: The introduction contrasts necessary resistance in war with an operation that lacked the forces and viability to achieve its aims.

segments.title: Operation Y-Go and the limits of delaying victory
segments.summary: Operation Y-Go is used to show that even a successful surprise attack on American carriers could only delay, not reverse, the Pacific war.
segments.body: Operation Y-Go echoed Pearl Harbor in its hope of catching American carriers in harbour, but the industrial balance of 1944 had changed the consequences. American carrier losses could be replaced in six to nine months, whereas Japan could not restore equivalent strength. British carrier construction also meant that Allied naval aviation was not confined to the American replacement programme. A surprise attack might buy Japan time to strengthen its defences, but it offered no credible path to reversing the war's outcome.

evidence.note: The lecture explains Y-Go, replacement capacity, and why a carrier strike could only delay the war.

segments.title: Kantai Kessen and the danger of planning for a foolish enemy
segments.summary: Kantai Kessen's failure warns against strategies that work only if the enemy keeps making mistakes.
segments.body: The Philippine Sea may have been the final opportunity to carry out Kantai Kessen, and its failure exposes the concept's weakness. A viable plan must assume a capable, committed opponent. It cannot depend on that opponent repeatedly advancing into an arranged trap. A strategy may fit one's own circumstances, but it must still account realistically for the enemy's intelligence, equipment, and will. Tan No. 2 instead demanded American complacency and perfect Japanese execution.

evidence.note: The lecture links Kantai Kessen to assumptions about enemy behaviour and strategic preparation.

segments.title: Operation Tan's small-strike problem
segments.summary: An earlier 54-aircraft plan against Majuro reveals how little margin Japan had for a surprise raid on a major anchorage.
segments.body: The original Operation Tan concept targeted Majuro, using reconnaissance from Truk followed by 27 torpedo bombers and 27 dive bombers. Its prospects depended on exceptional surprise and still offered no certainty of major results. Shallow-water torpedo attack required more than altering the torpedo itself. British practice at Taranto combined tail fins with a tension wire that made the weapon enter the water in a flatter attitude, and remnants were easy to overlook among cables and other debris after an air raid.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies Majuro as the target, describes the 54-aircraft concept, and explains the technical problem of torpedo attacks in harbour.

segments.title: C6N reconnaissance undone by serviceability
segments.summary: The C6N Saiun promised long-range reconnaissance, but the move to Truk left only one aircraft reliably available.
segments.body: The C6N was designed to overcome the limits of reconnaissance by cruiser floatplanes, but it required careful maintenance and specialized support. On 11 February 1945, seven aircraft left the Tokyo Bay area for Truk. Two turned back with engine trouble, one ditched en route, and another was wrecked on landing. Truk lacked the specialized servicing, fuel, and spares needed to keep the survivors available. The resulting reconnaissance plan depended on one serviceable aircraft and a submarine-delivered supply effort.

evidence.note: The lecture describes the C6N's role, the delivery losses, and the lack of maintenance support at Truk.

segments.title: Ulithi and the wrong scale for a penny-packet raid
segments.summary: Ulithi's immense anchorage exposes the mismatch between the American fleet base and Japan's small proposed raid.
segments.body: Ulithi had become a major forward base whose lagoon could hold about 1,000 large ships, with facilities including floating dry docks. Supply ships, tugs, escorts, cruisers, destroyers, battleships, and several types of carrier filled the anchorage. Counting only the carriers hid the depth of the force being targeted. A small force sent piecemeal against such a concentration would be expended without producing strategically meaningful damage, much as repeated small attacks fail once a defended opponent has concentrated strength.

evidence.note: The lecture describes Ulithi's facilities and fleet concentration, then criticizes penny-packet attacks.

segments.title: Optimism bias and serviceability planning
segments.summary: The C6N deployment shows why observed serviceability must determine force size and logistics.
segments.body: The plan assumed that every Japanese component would work while the American defenders remained unprepared. Actual C6N experience gave a stark warning: only one of seven dispatched reconnaissance aircraft was serviceable at Truk after losses, defects, and inadequate support. That observed rate should have driven force sizing and logistics calculations. Planners treated it as an exception. The intended targets were the carriers that enabled American amphibious operations, so ignoring measured readiness left the raid dependent on ideal conditions.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts the plan's perfect-performance assumptions with the roughly one-in-seven C6N serviceability actually observed.

segments.title: Tan No. 2's strike plan had no fuel margin
segments.summary: The planned 24 Ginga kamikaze strike depended on a long weather-avoidance route that made fuel itself part of the weapon's shortfall.
segments.body: The plan called for 24 P1Y Ginga bombers, five Kawanishi H8K flying boats for weather reconnaissance and guidance, and three submarines in support roles. The account is unclear about how many of the flying boats joined the main formation. Avoiding equatorial storms lengthened the route and consumed fuel before the aircraft reached Ulithi. A kamikaze aircraft's remaining fuel contributed to its impact, so the long route reduced both range margin and destructive effect. An unsuspecting anchorage would be no more alert against 240 or 480 aircraft than against 24. Japan needed to concentrate enough striking power to matter or abandon the raid. Against the fleet at Ulithi, 24 aircraft were neither a viable mass attack nor a force worth sacrificing in isolation.

evidence.note: The lecture outlines the P1Y and H8K force, the route, fuel burden, and inadequate strike size.

segments.title: Submarine support and rigid planning
segments.summary: The submarine plan added logistics, navigation, and rescue tasks while mechanical failures and rigid orders eroded its usefulness.
segments.body: Three submarines divided navigation, rescue, and supply duties, making the air operation dependent on another fragile chain. The 370-ton cargo submarine HA-106 waited off Minami Daito Jima, while the 1,779-ton transport submarine I-366 carried supplies toward Truk after receiving Type 13 air-search and Type 22 surface-search radar. I-366 had to return for repairs after its formal send-off. I-58 was recalled from a Kaiten mission about 90 minutes from its release point, forcing two Kaiten to be abandoned without any chance to attack. The recall shows how rigid adherence to the written plan displaced practical judgement about sequencing tasks and using forces already at hand.

evidence.note: The lecture details the submarine assignments, I-366's defects, and I-58's recall.

segments.title: Reconnaissance of Ulithi and a fragile launch
segments.summary: A C6N reconnaissance flight identified carriers at Ulithi, but bad weather and engine failures began dismantling the strike force on departure.
segments.body: The 5 March reconnaissance found Saratoga, four Essex-class carriers, three Independence-class carriers, seven escort carriers, and four unidentified ships at Ulithi. The C6N survived interception by three P-38 Lightnings, but the sighting confirmed the scale of the intended target. Bad weather delayed the H8K pathfinders on 11 March, and the Ginga launch fell behind schedule. Within hours, five aircraft had turned back and three had crashed, reducing the force before it approached the target.

evidence.note: The lecture covers the C6N sighting, the D-Day launch, weather delays, and early attrition.

segments.title: Navigation error, attrition, and the hit on USS Randolph
segments.summary: Engine trouble and a navigation error left only two aircraft at Ulithi, where one struck USS Randolph with little fuel remaining.
segments.body: At 13:20, I-58 detected the formation with Type 13 air-search radar and broadcast a continuous long-wave signal to help guide it. Engine trouble reduced the strike from 24 aircraft to eight before a navigation error near Yap, and only two reached Ulithi at 20:07 after almost eleven hours in the air. One P1Y hit the Essex-class carrier USS Randolph, killing 26 and wounding 105, but its fuel was so depleted that the aircraft did not burst into flames. The other aircraft crashed into a baseball field without damaging a military target. Japan paid for this temporary damage with roughly 60 to 70 personnel and at least 13 aircraft. Randolph returned for the Okinawa campaign, so the hit produced no durable operational result. The American anchorage had been caught napping, yet the understrength raid still failed.

evidence.note: The lecture recounts the losses, the navigation error, the Randolph strike, the Japanese cost, and the failure despite achieving surprise.

segments.title: Heavier bombers and the payload alternative
segments.summary: A counterfactual comparison with the Doolittle Raid asks whether larger bombers could have delivered enough fuel and explosives to threaten Ulithi's carriers.
segments.body: Merely sending more P1Y aircraft would still leave them almost dry at the end of the route. A more dangerous alternative might have adapted larger medium bombers in the manner of the American Doolittle Raid. Greater payload and residual fuel could have produced much more destructive impacts on carrier decks. This remains a counterfactual design argument, but it clarifies that the plan's weakness lay in weapon effect as well as aircraft numbers.

evidence.note: The lecture considers a Doolittle-style use of larger bombers carrying more explosives and fuel as an alternative strike design.

segments.title: Big Blue Blanket and carrier damage resilience
segments.summary: Okinawa's Big Blue Blanket and carrier damage images show how air defence, fuel, repeated impacts, and construction shaped kamikaze consequences.
segments.body: Images from Okinawa show the level of damage that the lightly fueled Randolph strike failed to produce. The Big Blue Blanket was an air-defence doctrine intended to give carrier task groups relative, though incomplete, safety. Bunker Hill suffered devastating damage from multiple kamikaze hits involving far more fuel. Essex-class construction is then compared with the greater structural resilience expected from a Midway-class or British armoured-hangar carrier. No carrier was invulnerable. Air defence, payload, number of hits, and protection determined whether an attack caused a lasting operational loss.

evidence.note: The lecture links the Big Blue Blanket's air-defence doctrine with Okinawa kamikaze damage and the protection of Essex, Midway, and British armoured-hangar carrier designs.

segments.title: Carrier resilience and the forlorn-hope test
segments.summary: The aftermath contrasts carrier resilience with a true forlorn hope: extreme risk is defensible only when it can unlock a concrete gain.
segments.body: Japanese reports initially imagined a second Pearl Harbor, but next-day reconnaissance from Truk found the carriers still present and no visible fuel in the water. The raid is compared with the British military tradition of the forlorn hope, whose volunteers accepted extreme danger to seize a wall and open the way for the main force. Participants received promotion because casualties were expected to be severe. A forlorn hope offered a concrete operational reward and could be divided into several assault parties when scale demanded it. Japan had more aircraft available, yet committed too few to make the risk operationally meaningful. Tan No. 2 had neither adequate resources nor a credible payoff. Its loss of life was strategically and morally indefensible.

evidence.note: The lecture covers the false expectation of a second Pearl Harbor and contrasts Tan No. 2 with a forlorn hope that could unlock a concrete military gain.
